modeling_assumptions.text: Appendix E's daily-rate projection: every hospitalization day from Day 2 onward is modeled at the real Dec 12/Dec 13 family-balance rate ($8,743.26/day), with no inflation, rate change, or new charge category beyond Dec 13. This is a disclosed simplification of a real hospital stay, not a sourced fact -- stated so every Hero's D1/D2 arithmetic starts from the same convention.

Appendix F's liquid/illiquid grouping (cash+brokerage vs. IRA/401k/pension vs. home/cars) is a stated modeling convention for which assets the case treats as available without a tax or timing penalty, not a claim about what a real family would necessarily choose to draw on first.

Household size for Appendix D's poverty-guideline lookup is left to the student to state and defend (Lily is a dependent living at home; Audrey and Caleb are away at college; Grace has her own household) -- the case does not resolve this itself, since a real hospital financial-assistance intake form would ask the family to state it, not assume it.

Extension of MA1's daily-rate convention, added 2026-08-18: if the family accepts a treatment option that moves Lauren out of ICU/ventilator care (e.g., home care), the $8,743.26/day ICU/ventilator rate stops accruing from that point forward -- it is billed only for days she is actually receiving ICU/ventilator care. Whatever alternative care setting she moves to is billed separately and is not part of this case's stated daily-rate figures. This is the convention that makes the twist's $150,000 treatment option a real financial comparison (an up-front cost against bill days the family would otherwise still be paying) rather than a pure addition on top of an unchanged ongoing daily rate. Surfaced in case.md Appendix E (student-facing); previously stated only in FACILITATOR.md -- see QA_REPORT.md 2026-08-18 entry for the P4 twist-integrity defect this closes.

deliverables.text: A day-by-day hospital bill ledger, starting from Appendix A's real Dec 11-13 bills and extended using Appendix E's daily rate through the exact date the chosen position ends.
A total out-of-pocket cost calculation for the position taken, with the addition and multiplication shown.
The percent of a typical day's hospital charge covered by insurance vs. left as the family's balance, and what having no out-of-pocket maximum means for that percent over time.
An assets map: which Net Worth Worksheet line items the family draws on, in what order, and the running liquid balance after each day's bill.
The exact day (and calendar date) the cumulative bill first exceeds (a) liquid assets and (b) total net worth, with the arithmetic shown and the day count rounded to a whole day.
An original visual display comparing the Escovedos' asset composition against the cumulative hospital bill at Day 14, Day 21, and Day 50.

balance.argument_a: The family's own liquid cash ($80,942.75) is exhausted by Day 10; adding the taxable brokerage account only extends that to Day 14 -- the LOW end of Dr. Halbert's own stated most-likely survival window (14-21 days), not a distant tail case. By Day 26 -- well inside the doctor's stated 50-day outer bound -- the cumulative bill exceeds the family's entire net worth ($218,368.19). Removing life support sooner does not change Lauren's certain, terminal prognosis or her <5% wake chance; it stops a real, uncapped, mounting bill from consuming savings a 14-year-old still at home may need.
balance.argument_b: In the doctor's own TYPICAL case, the family is not actually facing guaranteed ruin: their liquid-asset runway (~13.5 days) is within ~3.4% of the doctor's stated 14-day low end. Even in the full 50-day worst case, the family's TOTAL assets ($667,756.51) exceed the worst-case bill (~$430,908.65) -- they would not have to sell the house, and retain real (if tax- and penalty-bearing) capacity in retirement accounts before the bill outruns everything they own. Keeping Lauren connected preserves the real, if small, chance she wakes again (which she briefly does, per the Twist) and gives Grace, still in transit from Los Angeles, time with her mother she would not otherwise get.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric: the family's liquid-asset (cash + taxable brokerage) runway in days, compared with the low end of Dr. Halbert's stated most-likely survival estimate (14 days). Runway = 1 + (111,953.63 - 2,488.91) / 8,743.26 = 13.52 days. Margin = |14 - 13.52| / 14 = 3.43%. This deliberately is NOT the raw dollar gap between 'stop immediately' and 'go the full 50 days' -- that gap is real, large, and disclosed (it is what D1-D5 make students compute), but by construction Option A's cost is always smaller than Option B's for any later stopping date, so it can never honestly be forced within SPEC's 20% cap the way the liquid-runway-vs-doctor's-estimate coincidence can. See legacy_conversion_note.
balance.stability: NOT stable. Verdict flips under a +-50% flex of either stated dial the primary metric depends on: daily_rate (Appendix E) at -50% moves runway to 26.04 days, flipping the winner from B to A at an 86.0% margin; survival_low_days (Appendix C) at -50% moves the doctor's reference point to 7.0 days, also flipping to A at a 93.1% margin. (The +50% direction on either dial does not flip the winner but still breaks the SPEC Section 2 20% cap -- 49.8% and 55.3% respectively.) twist_treatment_cost is stable across its full +-50% range (margin stays 3.6%, no flip) because the Twist's diagnostics do not feed the A/B metric itself. This instability is NOT a case-design defect to retune away: the primary metric was deliberately chosen (see margin_basis) because it is a genuinely close, REAL coincidence between two legacy-preserved facts -- the real billed daily rate (Appendix E) and the doctor's own stated survival estimate (Appendix C) -- neither of which can be altered without breaking the legacy_conversion_note's verbatim-preservation guarantee. A metric this close by construction cannot also be flex-stable; narrowing it further would mean picking a less honest metric. Both unstable dials carry Category-F sensitivity_disclosure[] entries with real justifications (irreducible forecast uncertainty -- a projected future billing rate and a physician's estimate range, neither researchable to a firmer number). Per the 2026-08-13 disclosure-aware-pass-state amendment to tier2_probes.py, a genuinely unstable dial that is disclosed this way -- category, param, and a real justification on file -- passes Tier 2 probe 5 as PASS_DISCLOSED, not FAIL; this supersedes the earlier DOCTRINE_LEDGER.md MCS-26/MCS-41 text (written before that amendment existed), which is stale on this point. Recorded in qa.tier2.P5 and FACILITATOR.md. See cases/end-of-life/sensitivity_model.py FLEX sweep for the full table.

legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y1/Session 6/End Of Life/Case Study_ End Of Life.docx, Guide Notes.docx, and three real bill PDFs) is a fictional-patient case built on a REAL hospital's billing-statement template. The three bill PDFs (Bill 12_11_20.pdf, 12_12_20.pdf, 12_13_20.pdf) and the Net Worth Worksheet images embedded in the source docx are preserved VERBATIM as this case's Appendix A and Appendix B dollar figures -- every charge, payment, adjustment, and balance in Appendix A, and every asset/liability line in Appendix B, is copied exactly as it appeared in the legacy source. One change was made for real-entity-safety, not accuracy: the legacy bill template's masthead used a real hospital's actual name and logo (a real, currently-operating Cleveland-area hospital system) as an artifact of a scrubbed real-world billing-statement template. Since the dollar figures attached to it are entirely fictional (a fictional patient, 'Lauren Escovedo', was never actually treated or billed by that real institution), keeping the real name risked implying a real hospital produced these specific charges. The hospital name was changed to a fictional one ('Lakeside Regional Medical Center') everywhere in case.md; no dollar figure, date, or line-item description was altered. The bill template's own Federal Poverty Guideline table (family-of-1 $10,890 / family-of-4 $22,350) was a stale figure inherited from whatever year the original scrubbed template dated to -- it did not match any real year's HHS guidelines and was not a number this case's narrative depends on being current, so it was replaced with the real, current 2026 HHS guidelines (Appendix D, cited S1), rather than either inventing a plausible-looking table or leaving a stale real-looking one in place. The legacy Challenge's four required outputs (removal date if Position A, total hospital cost, which assets pay it, whether/when the family runs out of money) are preserved as the spine of D1-D5; D3 (insurance-coverage percent) and D6 (visual display) were added to force real, distinct standards (percent-of-a-number; pie chart) the original four questions didn't independently reach on their own, and to satisfy Challenge 2's own visual-display requirement with a genuine deliverable rather than treating it as decorative. The original Guide Notes' Twist content (a doctor's call that Lauren has briefly woken; a separate, undated, internally-inconsistent set of experimental-treatment costs -- $120,000 in the Guide Notes' main body, then $200,000 and $400,000 with different survival/quality-of-life terms in its own 'Lessons Learned' section, with no reconciliation given) could not be preserved as a single sourced figure: the source itself never settles on one number or one set of terms. Rather than silently picking one of the three conflicting legacy figures and presenting it as though the source had settled on it, FACILITATOR.md authors ONE internally-consistent twist (Lauren briefly wakes, then a $150,000 experimental treatment -- insurance won't cover it, and it does not change Dr. Halbert's original 50-day outer bound) built fresh from this conversion's own real cost-per-day rate, disclosed here as authored rather than sourced. The primary_metric and margin_pct required a genuine design decision, documented under 'balance' above and FACILITATOR.md's sensitivity note: a naive 'total cost of stopping now vs. total cost of the full 50 days' metric is real and large but can never honestly clear SPEC's 20% balance cap, because Option A's cost is definitionally smaller than a later Option B stopping point -- the same category of problem Cardiology's conversion hit with its $67,000 real cost gap. Following that precedent, this conversion instead declares a different, genuinely close, real metric (liquid-asset runway vs. the doctor's own low-end survival estimate, a real 3.43% gap) as the graded primary metric, while keeping the large, real, fully disclosed total-cost gap central to the Challenge's own deliverables (D1, D2, D4, D5) rather than hiding it.
sensitivity_note: Real end-of-life care decision for a fictional family facing a life-support choice, built on top of a real hospital billing-statement format and real, current federal poverty guidelines (SPEC.md §6). The stake here is financial protection and family time, not a casualty count -- keep the discussion frame on the family's own real numbers (the bill ledger, the net-worth worksheet, the doctor's stated survival window), not on personal end-of-life anecdotes from the room, which this kind of case can surface unexpectedly. Flag this case to a facilitator before running it with any cohort where a recent family loss is known.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The billing rate assumes no inflation or rate change beyond the last billed day -- a real family-balance rate projected forward. How medical costs would actually change over a multi-week stay is genuinely unknowable in advance, the same as any future-cost forecast.

A physician's survival estimate for a specific patient is inherently a range, not a certainty, in real medicine -- doctors give estimates precisely because the true outcome cannot be known in advance. This is irreducible forecast uncertainty, not a research gap the case failed to close.
